summary: Five parallel approaches to raise Stage 1 recall at bounded false alarms

result.approach:
I added causal pose cues for the littering act, computed per stitched track with pure numpy on boxes and keypoints. I first dumped per-person cue features for littering actors, bystanders and normal Avenue footage to see which cues separate them. I then swept thresholds and persistence through score(combine(baseline, method)) on the tune halves.

Cues I built:
- extend: horizontal wrist-to-same-shoulder distance divided by the track's median body height.
- low: wrist below the hip line.
- raise: wrist above the shoulder.
- swing: wrist speed relative to the shoulder/hip centre over a ~0.3 s lag, with a minimum displacement.
- outside: wrist outside the torso's horizontal span.
- bend: torso shortening against the track median.
- crouch: box height shrinking against the track median.
- I also logged forearm angle, elbow straightness and reach distance for analysis.

Two things made the cues usable:
1. Per-cue persistence: a cue must hold in N frames within the window. The window stretches at low fps so the 1 fps smoking footage still works. This cut keypoint-jitter false alarms roughly in half for the same recall.
2. Suppression against the baseline: if the baseline already sent this person in the last 2.5 s, the cue does not fire again. This only looks at baseline events at or before t, so it stays causal.

Dedup is once per person per 5 s cooldown. The ROI is the firing person's own box, which is the actor rather than a bystander. Nothing is fitted, and ground truth is never read inside the method.
result.summary:
I built littering_act.py, which exposes make_method(**params) and DEFAULTS (DEFAULTS is operating point C). It adds pose cues for the littering act on top of the baseline rules.

The two cues that work are:
- arm held out sideways or forward: wrist at least 0.16 to 0.18 body heights horizontally from its shoulder, sustained for 3 frames;
- hand below the hip line: sustained for 4 frames.

Overhand raise (wrist above shoulder, 3 frames) is an extra option. It mainly helps throwing and Avenue.

All numbers are combine(baseline, method) on the tune halves:
- **Point C (recommended):** littering event recall goes from 75.7 to 91.3 and crop recall from 52.2 to 70.0. Avenue event recall goes from 76 to 96 and crop from 60 to 72. Normal false alarms rise from 7.05 to 14.69 per minute (+7.6).
- **Cheapest point A (+2.75 FA/min):** already gives littering crop recall 66.5 and event recall 87.0.
- **Per action:** throwing crop recall rises from 30.4 to 63 to 74, and dropping from 32.6 to 56.5. Tossing only rises from 26.1 to 37, and remains the hardest action.

Smoking barely moves (+1 to 2 points), as expected.

result.recommended:
I recommend point C (the module's DEFAULTS). It raises littering crop recall from 52.2 to 70.0 and event recall from 75.7 to 91.3. It also raises Avenue event recall from 76 to 96, for about +7.6 candidates per minute on normal footage.

Use A if the false-alarm budget is tight: it gets most of the gain (crop recall 66.5) for only +2.75 per minute. Use D if catching throwing matters more than VLM load: it brings Avenue crop recall to 88 and throwing crop recall to 74, at +11 per minute.
result.what_failed:
- **Wrist-swing speed relative to the torso** barely helped littering. The littering clips' assumed 10 fps is too coarse for a throw, and actors' peak speeds overlapped with bystanders and walkers. At 1.0 body heights per second it gave littering crop recall only 56.5 while normal false alarms rose to 19 per minute. It did help Avenue (event recall 96), so it is kept in the module but turned off.
- **Torso bend and crouch** gave no littering gain, and crouch was noisy on normal footage.
- **The wrist-outside-the-torso cue** was no better than plain arm extension.
- **Raising the keypoint-confidence threshold** to 0.5 or 0.7, and changing the minimum person height between 40 and 90 px, made little difference.
- **Wider ROIs** ("person+ground", or grouping with neighbouring people) gave zero crop-recall gain.
- **A longer cooldown** would not help: every false alarm at point A came from a different person.
- **Dropping and tossing remain largely invisible to pose.** Looking at missed clips, the actor is walking with the arm hanging and the item just falls. Some clips also have tiny people whose keypoints are unusable. Pose cues are close to their ceiling on these actions.
- **A raw height filter is not a real fix.** It cuts false alarms to near zero only because Avenue's people are small (about 113 px) while littering actors are large (about 290 px). That is a dataset artefact, so I did not use it.
result.risks:
- **Small, noisy false-alarm estimate.** The normal set is only 5.1 minutes, so each extra candidate moves the rate by 0.2 per minute. Point A's +2.75 per minute is about 14 extra candidates, so these rates are only roughly known.
- **Lower VLM-load reduction on Avenue.** It falls from 43% to 25% (A), 17% (C) and 10% (D) on the anomaly videos, because each new candidate adds a 5 s window. This is a real increase in VLM load beyond the normal-footage false-alarm rate.
- **Thresholds were swept on the tune half only.** The held-out half has not been checked. The persistence counts and body-height thresholds were chosen from fairly few events (about 46 clips per action), so expect a few points of shrinkage.
- **Domain shift.** Cues are normalised by body height, but keypoint noise depends on pixel size. Small people on new CCTV may trigger more false alarms, and the littering clips are 1080p handheld footage, not fixed CCTV.
- **Causality.** The method uses only past frames for both the track history and the check against baseline candidates. The baseline replay cache is only a speed-up for sweeps.
- **Cost.** A few numpy operations per person per frame, no new models.

result.approach: One-class kNN model of normal people's poses. Each pose is normalised to the body: joints are measured from the shoulder/hip midpoint and divided by torso length, with a box-based fallback. Missing joints are masked out of the distance. The normal bank also holds mirror images. It is fitted ONLY on SPLITS["normal"] (tune half), with leave-one-video-out for normal FA and per-channel calibration. Scores are computed per channel and take the max; the channels used are vertical-only joint coordinates plus leg x/y. A candidate needs persistence (k hits in 1 s; one hit is enough on low-fps sources) and fires once per stitched person per 15 s.
result.summary:
I built /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ianvarella-capstone-S25/34f35ddd-aadf-47db-aeef-bab5602d89b5/scratchpad/exp/pose_anomaly.py. It exposes make_method(**params), DEFAULTS (= point B) and OPERATING_POINTS {A, B, C}.

Features and model:
- Each person with keypoints becomes 13 joints (nose, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles). Coordinates are measured from the shoulder/hip midpoint and divided by torso length, floored at 0.15 x box height.
- Joints below 0.3 confidence are masked out of the distance. Mean-filling covers the missing joints in the bank.
- The bank holds 4000 normal vectors (2000 people plus their mirror images), drawn only from the normal tune videos.
- Score: RMS distance to the 5 nearest normal vectors, per channel, divided by that channel's 99th percentile on leave-one-video-out normal scores. So 1.0 means "as unusual as the top 1% of normal people".
- Channels used: "body_y" (vertical coordinates of all joints, which don't change with which way the person faces) and "legs" (x/y of hips, knees, ankles).
- A candidate fires when the score is at or above threshold on min_hits observations of that person within 1 s. One hit is enough if that person's previous observation is more than 0.5 s old, which covers 1 fps smoking. After firing, that stitched person (TrackStitcher, same as the current rules) is quiet for 15 s. The ROI is the person box grown by 0.25 x height.

Rule compliance:
- Fully causal: only past frames of the same tracker id are used.
- Never reads gt.
- Fitted only on SPLITS["normal"] tune.
- Normal FA is scored with leave-one-video-out banks, because a kNN would otherwise match each frame to itself.
- Cost is about 0.5 ms/frame on Avenue (6.3 people/frame) in numpy.

result.what_failed:
- Velocity features (joint motion relative to the body, 1-frame or 0.3/0.5 s lag, in the same kNN or as separate arm/body velocity channels) hurt. Keypoint jitter on 640x360 Avenue (people about 110 px tall) makes normal people look like they're moving unusually: e.g. body+arms+armvel at thr 1.0 gave avenue 100% but normal FA 33/min. At 1 fps (smoking) no velocity can be computed at all. The arm-swing idea does not survive this keypoint quality.
- Full x/y pose channels were worse than vertical-only ones at the same FA. In Avenue nearly everyone walks across the frame side-on, while littering and smoking cameras see people facing them, so x coordinates mostly measure which way a person faces rather than odd behaviour.
- Stretching the normal bank horizontally to fake other viewpoints (x1.8, x2.8) lowered Avenue recall and gave no net gain.
- A "self-novelty" score (current pose versus the same person's last 2.5 s) did not tell littering actors from bystanders either.
- k=1/10, bank 12k, cal_q 0.995 and cooldown 30 s were all within noise of the chosen settings.
- min_hits 2-5 within 1 s let thresholds go lower and was clearly better than single-frame firing.
- Diagnostic: in littering clips the actor's highest score was above everyone else's in only 36% of clips. Bending actions (dumping, putting-down) score high but are already caught by reach_down; for dropping, throwing and tossing the actor is no more unusual to the model than the bystanders.
- Random-firing control at matched cost:
  - Littering: random firing adding 7.4 candidates/min gave 83.0/59.6, versus A's 89.1/69.1 while adding only 5.9/min.
  - Smoking: at a matched candidate rate, random gave 54.5/25.4 versus A's 64.6/32.4.
  - Avenue: random firing costing +3.1 FA/min gave 84/60, versus A's 88/68 at +2. Avenue events are long and crowded, so firing on random people there is almost as good.
  - So there is real signal, but it is modest.
result.risks:
Domain shift is the main risk. Normal FA is only measured on the Avenue camera the model was fitted on. On other cameras people look more unusual to the model just because of the viewpoint, so the method fires more there, and part of the littering and smoking recall gain is paid for with extra review load the FA metric doesn't count:
- Smoking review reduction drops from 55.6% to 34.7% (A), 27.7% (B) and 26.8% (C), meaning roughly 1.5-1.6x as many smoking frames go to the VLM.
- Littering candidates per minute rise from 28.0 to 33.9 (A) and 37.6 (B).

On a new site, expect normal false alarms well above the Avenue figure until the bank includes normal footage from that camera. Re-fitting per camera on a few minutes of normal video is the obvious fix, and it is cheap.

Other risks:
- Overfitting: thresholds and persistence were picked on tune-half recall (25 Avenue events, 230 littering clips, about 58 smoking events), so each Avenue event is worth 4 points. Check A/B/C on the held-out half before choosing.
- Larger crops: roi_grow 0.25 adds about 2-4 crop points at no FA cost, but sends the VLM larger crops (person plus surroundings), and it partly inflates the box_hit metric.
- Low fps: on 1 fps footage a single high frame fires a candidate, which is part of why smoking load grows.
- Missing keypoints: people without keypoints (about 10-20%), or with fewer than 8 visible joints, are never scored.
- Leave-one-out FA uses 7-video banks, while deployment uses all 8, so live normal FA may be slightly lower.
- Cost: about 0.5 ms/frame.

result.approach: I built id-robust person tracks and added two cues. The first is a per-camera "rare presence" model fitted on normal footage. The second is a stricter speed rule that runs on those re-linked tracks. Linker: when ByteTrack gives a new raw id, it is attached to a track lost less than 0.6 s ago if its constant-velocity prediction lands within 0.6 body-heights (h), or if the raw jump is under 3.5 h/s, and the box heights are within 0.7 to 1.43x. This matters because the Avenue runner in test/03 gets a new tracker id almost every frame, so the baseline speed rule never sees 4 consecutive points. Fast cue: median step speed, capped at 1.25x the net displacement, divided by the 75th-percentile height of the track. Boxes clipped by the left or right frame edge are ignored, and the cue re-arms only after the person slows down. Density cue: a smoothed 4-D histogram over (foot x, foot y, log box height / frame height, speed class still/walk/fast), 16x16x10x3 bins with a +-1-bin box filter. It is fitted only on SPLITS["normal"] (tune half). It fires when a person's density stays below the q-th quantile of normal person-frames for 5 consecutive observations of the track. This catches people unusually close to the camera, in places people never are, or standing still where people only walk past. When scoring "normal", the model is refitted leave-one-video-out, so the false-alarm figure is out-of-sample. Dedup: at most 1 candidate per track per 2 s. Density re-fires every 3 s at most, with a backoff by location: each re-fire at the same place (IoU >= 0.4) doubles the wait, up to 48 s, which stops static false detections and people standing near the camera from spamming. Everything is causal, uses no ground truth, and costs about 0.3 ms per frame in pure Python/numpy. The scene cues run only for the Avenue camera ("avenue" and "normal"), because littering and smoking have no normal footage of their cameras.
result.summary: I wrote motion_anomaly.py, exposing make_method(**params) and DEFAULTS. It finds two kinds of Avenue anomaly the baseline misses. The first is people somewhere normal footage almost never has them: very close to the camera, at odd positions, or standing still where people normally walk past. A smoothed histogram of normal footage defines "rare" (normal-only fit; false alarms measured leave-one-video-out). The second is runners whose tracker id keeps changing, caught by re-linking those ids into one track and applying a strict 3 body-heights/s speed rule. Results are for combine(baseline, method) on the tune half. Avenue crop recall goes from 60.0 to 92.0 and event recall from 76.0 to 96.0, for +2.2 false alarms per minute on normal (7.05 to 9.21). The new candidates are as precise as the baseline's (Avenue candidate precision 36.7% to 38.0%). Littering and smoking are unchanged, as expected. There are no gains on those sets, and nothing gets worse. The main cost is that Avenue review reduction falls from 43.2% to 21.1%: the VLM gets about 79% of Avenue test frames instead of 57%. Of the 10 events the baseline missed on Avenue tune, 8 are now caught: 6 near-camera or odd-position people (test/09, 11, 15, 17 twice, 19), 1 runner with id switches (test/03) and 1 running/odd entry (test/01). The 2 still missed: in test/13 at 10.3 s, an ordinary-looking person walking in at the left edge whose ground-truth box is much wider than the person (probably carrying or pushing something); and in test/13 at 18.3 s, an object thrown in the air that YOLO never detects (the clip is already flagged in time, but the crop misses it).

result.recommended: The "recommended" point (DEFAULTS: fast at 3.0 h/s plus density at quantile 0.005). It costs only about 2 false alarms per minute over the baseline (one candidate every ~28 s of normal footage). Avenue crop recall goes from 60 to 92% and event recall from 76 to 96%. The new candidates are no less precise than the baseline's. If missing an event matters much more than VLM load, use "high-recall" (q=0.02) at +5.3 FA/min, which reaches 100/96. The quantile threshold is used instead of a fixed density value because it holds up when the bin size changes (see risks).
result.what_failed: These cues added nothing on the tune half. Wrong-direction walking (per-cell direction histogram fitted on normal, needing 1 s of a rare heading) never fired usefully, with 0 gain at wrong_p of 0.03 and 0.08; the wrong-direction anomalies are either already caught or not in the odd-numbered videos. Thrown objects via item tracks (bag or bottle moving fast or upwards): COCO items reach at most about 0.45 frame-heights/s on Avenue and the thrown papers or bag are never detected, so 0 gain at every threshold tried. Turn/zig-zag detection: +4 event recall, 0 crop recall, +3.5 FA/min; mostly linker and box jitter. A per-cell size model ("taller than the 99th percentile for this cell"): almost no gain, because the 6-row grid lumps bottom-row people together. It was replaced by the density model. A rare-location-only model (occupancy grid, no height or speed): +12 crop recall but +3.5 FA/min, and it repeatedly fired on a static false detection at the left edge of test/01. The 4-D density, hold and backoff fixed that. A lower speed threshold on re-linked tracks (1.2 to 2.0 h/s): +5 to +6.5 FA/min, because jittery boxes and partly detected people inflate the speed of normal walkers. Only at 2.5 to 3 h/s does it become cheap, about +0.4 FA/min. A density model without the speed dimension did worse (80 crop at the same false-alarm cost). No smoothing (dens_smooth=0) gave 35 FA/min.
result.risks: 1. Small tune set. Avenue tune has only 25 events in 11 videos, and the gain comes from about 6 videos with people close to the camera. Normal tune is only about 5 minutes (8 videos), so 1 candidate equals 0.2 FA/min, and the FA figures carry large relative error. 2. Threshold sensitivity. With a fixed density threshold, results move a lot with bin size (14 bins gave 80 crop, 16 bins gave 92). The quantile threshold is steadier: 88 to 96 crop at q=0.005 and 96 for all bin sizes at q=0.02, but expect some drop on the held-out half. 3. Review load. Avenue review reduction falls from 43% to 21% (14% at high-recall). Avenue test footage is anomaly-dense (27% positive frames) and contains static large people, and the location backoff only partly limits repeats. This shows up as VLM cost, not as normal-footage false alarms. 4. Domain shift. The density and direction models are per camera and need normal footage from each deployed camera. They are disabled for littering and smoking, which have none, so this method does nothing for those sets. A deployment needs a calibration pass of normal video per camera, and the model goes stale if the camera moves. 5. Causality. Features use only the past; the model is fitted offline on normal video only; ground truth is never read; held-out data was never touched. 6. The linker can mislink people in crowds. That is why the speed threshold has to stay high (3 h/s), and lower speeds are left to the baseline rule. 7. Scratch scripts are in the same exp directory. My explore1.py to explore4.py may share a directory with other agents' files. The module itself does not depend on them.

result.approach: Pose-free "person stays in an area" candidates for smoking at about 1 fps. Dwell is timed on position spots, meaning foot positions that keep being occupied by some person box whatever its tracker id, with gaps allowed (spot_keep_s). It is not timed on tracker IDs, because at 1 fps 66% of smoking GT events fall on a person's first frame under a new raw tracker id. Rules: (1) dwell: the spot has been occupied for at least dwell_s=1 s and the person moved less than still_h=0.5 body heights since then. Each stationary spot is re-sampled at most once per cooldown_s of wall time. (2) first_seen snapshot: a brand-new spot away from the frame border gets one snapshot. (3) optional reseen: a stationary spot that was not observed for 2 s or more is re-sampled early, with a floor of min_gap_s. Cost control: location dedupe (no candidate within dedupe_h body heights of one sent in the last cooldown), grouping (one candidate's ROI is the union of nearby stationary people, capped at 60% of frame width/height, so a group of workers costs one VLM call), and an optional per-minute budget. Pure python/numpy on boxes, about 0.07 to 0.24 ms per frame. Nothing is fitted on data. Causal: each candidate is stamped at its decision frame and uses only earlier observations. I tuned only on the tune half (random plus focused grids, about 3,000 configs on smoking and normal) and read no GT inside the method.
result.summary:
I built smoking_dwell.py, a pose-free module that exposes make_method(**params), DEFAULTS (the recommended B_mid point) and OPERATING_POINTS (the Pareto set below). All numbers are for combine(baseline, method) on the tune half.

At about +6 normal false alarms per minute (B_mid), smoking event recall goes from 43.1% to 77.4% and crop recall from 17.2% to 48.7%. The share of smoking sequences with at least one correct crop goes from 39.5% to 74.8%. Smoking candidates per minute go from 4.8 to 11.8, and candidate precision on smoking actually rises, from 17.8% to 23.5%.

The pieces that matter, from ablations at B_mid:
- **Grouping** adds about 6 crop points and saves about 4 false alarms per minute.
- **The first-seen snapshot** adds about 6.5 event points and about 8 sequence points.
- **Location dedupe** is essential. Without it the false alarms jump to about 47 per minute.
- **Spots vs tracker IDs:** spot association beats TrackStitcher canonical IDs by about 4 event points. Raw IDs are about the same as spots once dedupe and grouping are on.

On a continuous stream the cost is the same or lower. When I joined the 8 normal clips into one stream (to remove the cost of each clip's start), the extra false alarms were 1.96, 4.69 and 6.06 per minute for A_lean, B_mid and C_recall.

Supporting files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ianvarella-capstone-S25/34f35ddd-aadf-47db-aeef-bab5602d89b5/scratchpad/exp/:
- verify.py: harness scores for every point.
- final.py: ablations.
- concat.py: the continuous-stream false-alarm estimate.
- diag2.py: why smoking events are missed.
- sweep_lib.py: fast cached scorer.
- sweep5.py, sweep6.py, sweep7.py: the parameter sweeps.

Littering per_action, baseline vs combine(baseline, A_lean), as event%/crop%:
- dropping: 60.9/32.6 to 100/95.7
- dumping: 100/97.8 to 100/100
- putting-down: 82.6/73.9 to 100/93.5
- throwing: 63.0/30.4 to 100/93.5
- tossing: 71.7/26.1 to 100/97.8

Don't credit this method with these gains. The littering clips are 3 s long and start with the litterer in view, so a 1 s stillness check plus a first-seen snapshot fires on essentially everyone in every clip. The jump is an artifact of the clip length, not a littering detector. The method does not target littering.
result.recommended:
B_mid, set as DEFAULTS. It is pose-free and costs +6.1 false alarms per minute on the per-clip harness, or +4.7 on the continuous stream. It nearly doubles smoking event recall (43 to 77%), almost triples crop recall (17 to 49%) and lifts sequence-level coverage from 40 to 75%. Candidate precision on smoking goes up.

Unlike the C points, it does not use the reseen trigger. That trigger mostly exploits the sampling gaps in the Roboflow smoking set, which are also exactly where the metric splits GT events. B_mid also does not collapse Avenue review reduction: it stays at 33%, against 11% for C_recall.

If recall must be pushed further, use C_recall (84.6/59.2, +8.6 FA/min). Accept that on busy 12.5 fps scenes it forwards about 89% of frames.

If false alarms must stay near the baseline, use A_lean (64.1/36.4, +1.6 FA/min).
result.what_failed:
- **Plain short-dwell re-sampling** (no dedupe or grouping) fails: it reaches 89% smoking event recall, but normal false alarms go to 60-200 per minute. Avenue has people standing for whole clips, and spots break up around them during crowd crossings and occlusion.
- **Tightening stillness doesn't separate the cases.** Even at still_h=0.05 the false alarms stay at 40 per minute or more, because Avenue's standing people really are still.
- **Longer dwell (3-6 s)** loses most of the smoking gain, because the sequences are short and sparse.
- **The reacquired trigger** (tracker id changes at a stationary spot) costs +25-30 FA/min, because Avenue tracks break in crowds.
- **The reseen trigger without a budget** costs +15-25 FA/min.
- **A per-minute budget alone**, without grouping, is clearly worse than grouping: at budget 2/min it reaches 58/28 at about +3 FA/min.
- **The lenient pose cue** (separate variant: wrist above shoulder or within 0.25 h of the head) added nothing on top of B_mid: 77.2/48.5 vs 77.4/48.7.
- **Canonical TrackStitcher IDs** were slightly worse than position spots (about -1 to -4 event points). Raw IDs were about the same once dedupe and grouping were on.

Remaining misses for B_mid (220 of 429 events):
- 149: the person was stationary but was sampled within the cooldown. These are mostly later fragments of the same smoking session after a gap, so the VLM had already seen this person.
- 30: a new spot was suppressed (frame edge or dedupe).
- 28: a candidate fired but its crop missed the smoker.
- 9: no person box was detected.
- 4: the person was moving.
result.risks:
- **Cost at 1 fps is not measured by the false-alarm metric.** Normal false alarms come only from 12.5 fps Avenue footage, where a walker keeps one spot. At 1 fps a walker jumps more than 0.5 h between frames and creates a new interior spot almost every frame, so first_seen also fires on walkers. The honest cost signal at 1 fps is smoking review reduction (55.6 to 23.8% at B_mid) and smoking candidates per minute (4.8 to 11.8). That means more VLM calls per camera on the smoking site.
- **The smoking set's gaps are a dataset artifact.** They come from frames sampled into the Roboflow dataset, not from a gappy live camera, and the metric splits GT events at those same gaps. So reseen and short cooldowns partly game the event count. In continuous deployment, expect the C points to gain less over B_mid. Sequence-level coverage (74.8 vs 84.9) is the less gap-sensitive number.
- **The test clips are short.** Normal clips average 38 s, so 30-60 s cooldowns barely recur. The continuous-stream check (joined clips) gave the same or lower cost, but that is still only 5.1 min of normal footage: +2 FA/min is about 10 candidates, so the false-alarm numbers are noisy.
- **Littering gains are a clip-length artifact**, not detection (see per_action).
- **Overfitting:** about 3,000 configs were searched on 429 smoking events. Expect a few points of optimism on the held-out half, which I did not run. Prefer the rounded B_mid parameters over the sweep's top cells.
- **Grouped crops are large.** Group ROIs are a median 5-6% of the frame on smoking, but about 20% on crowded Avenue (union of several people). The VLM gets less-localised crops, and with group_max_frac=1.0 a crop could approach the whole scene. I capped it at 0.6.
- **Fit and causality are fine:** nothing is fitted on data, and every rule is causal.

result.approach: I repackaged the existing baseline candidates. The baseline rule engine is replayed causally inside the method. Whenever a baseline reach_down candidate fires on person P at time t, the method also sends, at the same t, one crop for the other person who was most active just before t. Activity is that person's box-centre motion plus 2x their mean keypoint change relative to their own box, over the previous 0.5 s, keyed by tracker raw_id. Each person gets at most one extra crop per 5 s cooldown. I compared three policies: "each" (separate per-person crops), "union" (one group crop) and "expand" (the trigger box grown, optionally down to the floor). I also compared ranking neighbours by activity against ranking by distance. Separately, I added an optional cheap cue, a wrist-movement trigger: a person fires when a wrist moves at least X body heights relative to their own box within 0.5 s (30 s cooldown per person). Packaging alone cannot create event recall, because about 56 of the 230 littering clips have no candidate at all, and this trigger is the only way the module buys any. Nothing is fitted on data; every threshold was picked by sweeping on the tune half. I read ground truth only in the separate analysis scripts, never inside the method.
result.summary:
Module crop_policy.py exposes make_method(**params), DEFAULTS and crop_area_frac().

- **Why packaging helps.** In most crop failures the right person was already in the frame. Of 54 littering clips where a candidate was on time but the crop missed the actor, 52 had the actor detected in that same frame. Almost all of these were reach_down firing on a bystander.
- **Packaging alone (+2.35 FA/min).** Adding one crop for the most active other person per reach_down candidate fixes most of them:
  - littering crop recall 52.2 -> 71.3 (the most packaging could reach is about 74.8)
  - avenue crop 60 -> 68
  - smoking crop 17.2 -> 23.5
  - normal false alarms 7.05 -> 9.40/min
  - average crop area stays 6.6% of the frame, same as baseline crops.
- **Ranking matters.** Ranking by activity beats ranking by distance, for example littering 71.3 vs 68.7 and avenue 68 vs 60.
- **Union crops cost VLM detail.** They reach about the same recall (littering 67.8-72.6) but the average crop grows to 36-52% of the frame.
- **Wrist-movement trigger.** Adding it buys event recall: avenue event recall 76 -> 84 at a wrist threshold of 0.40 and 76 -> 92 at 0.36, and littering event recall 75.7 -> 79.6. The cost is more false alarms and more forwarded footage: avenue review reduction falls from 43.2% to 29.1% at 0.36.

Scripts and sweep CSVs (cp_*.py, cp_sweep_*.csv) are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ianvarella-capstone-S25/34f35ddd-aadf-47db-aeef-bab5602d89b5/scratchpad/exp/.

result.per_action:
Littering per action, event % / crop %. Baseline vs pack_k1 vs pack_k1_wrist0.36:
- dropping: 60.9/32.6 -> 60.9/60.9 -> 63.0/60.9
- dumping: 100/97.8 -> 100/100 -> 100/100
- putting-down: 82.6/73.9 -> 82.6/82.6 -> 84.8/84.8
- throwing: 63.0/30.4 -> 63.0/50.0 -> 73.9/58.7
- tossing: 71.7/26.1 -> 71.7/63.0 -> 76.1/65.2

Packaging fixes most of the crop gap for dropping and tossing. Throwing and tossing still lack event recall: about 25-37% of those clips get no candidate at all, and the wrist trigger only recovers part of it. With pack_k1, 66 littering events are still missed. Only 10 of those had a candidate at the right time, so the rest need a new trigger rather than better packaging.
result.recommended: Recommended: pack_k1_wrist0.36 (+7.45 false alarms/min), the module DEFAULTS, because recall is the priority. It gives the largest gains: littering crop recall 52.2 -> 73.9, avenue event recall 76 -> 92, and crop sizes stay as small as baseline (6.7% of the frame). If false alarms must stay under about +2.5/min, deploy pack_k1 instead (trigger_wrist=None). It is nearly free: +2.35/min, crop recall +19 points on littering, +8 on avenue and +6 on smoking, with no loss of review reduction.
result.what_failed:
- **Union crops.** They match the recall of separate crops but the crop grows to 36-52% of the frame. The area cap (max_area_frac) does not shrink it much, because one far neighbour already makes the union huge.
- **Expanding the trigger box.** Growing it by 0.5x or 1.0x, with or without extending it to the floor, reached only 54-62 littering crop recall at higher cost. The extra space at the feet changed nothing.
- **Ranking neighbours by distance.** It is worse than ranking by activity (littering 68.7 vs 71.3, avenue 60 vs 68).
- **Requiring a minimum activity before a neighbour gets a crop.** It hurts badly (littering crop falls to 53-63), because littering actors are often nearly still. It saved almost no false alarms.
- **Repackaging other rules.** Doing it for sustained_presence, fast_motion and unattended_object costs +2 to +3 FA/min for at most +0.5 smoking crop recall.
- **More than one neighbour crop.** k=2 or k=3 mainly helps smoking crop recall, at about +2.4 FA/min per extra neighbour.
- **Activity window and cooldown.** Sweeping the window (0.5/1/2 s) and the cooldown (2/5/10 s) barely mattered.
- **Pose-change trigger.** A mean keypoint-change trigger was worse than the wrist trigger: 0.15 gave 32 FA/min.
- **Remaining smoking misses.** About 84 smoking events had a candidate at the right time but no matching crop, and repackaging cannot fix most of them. Roughly 61 have the ground-truth smoker undetected as a person, and about 16 have a candidate window that overlaps but fires more than 1 s away from a labelled frame. Event recall on smoking stays around 43-44%.
result.risks:
- **Wrist threshold is sensitive.** False alarms go 20.4 / 14.5 / 11.8 per minute at thresholds 0.33 / 0.36 / 0.40.
- **Avenue tune half is small.** It has only about 25 events, so one event is 4 points, and the 76 -> 92 avenue jump is 4 events. It needs checking on the held-out half.
- **The wrist trigger cuts review reduction.** Avenue review reduction falls from 43.2% to 29.1% at 0.36, and from 43.2% to 33.9% at 0.40.
- **Wrist trigger sizes are in body heights relative to the box.** That makes it roughly independent of scale, but pose-keypoint jitter on small, low-resolution people in other cameras could raise false alarms. It may also duplicate an arm-swing rule built separately.
- **Normal footage is crowded.** Normal Avenue has about 8 people per frame, so packaging adds a crop on essentially every reach_down candidate; the extra false alarms come from how many such candidates there are, not from how many neighbours.
- **Two candidates per moment.** When the deployed system sends them, the VLM workload per moment roughly doubles. A real deployment could instead attach the neighbour crop to the same candidate, which would make the extra false alarms nearly zero. The harness counts each crop as a separate candidate, so the numbers here are the pessimistic case.
- **Causality and cost.** The method replays the baseline engine frame by frame and uses only past observations. The per-frame work is a few numpy operations per visible person, and nothing is fitted on data. Ground truth was read only in the separate analysis scripts, never in the method.
